cards.title: Hash Function
cards.teaser: The machine that turns any key into an array index — and why three properties make or break it.

runs.text: A hash function takes an arbitrary key — a string, an integer, a tuple — and returns a non-negative integer called a
(or digest). That integer is then reduced to an array index, typically via modulo:
. This is the entire trick behind O(1) lookup — instead of scanning a list for a key, you compute where it must be.
A good hash function has three mandatory properties:

items.text: the same key always produces the same hash value. If this breaks, lookup becomes impossible.
outputs spread evenly across the possible index space, minimizing collisions. A hash that maps every key to index 0 is technically deterministic but catastrophically slow.
computing the hash must be cheaper than the cost it's trying to avoid. A hash function slower than a linear scan defeats the purpose.

runs.text: uses SipHash-1-3 for strings and bytes (since Python 3.4) — a fast, cryptographically influenced function that resists hash-flooding denial-of-service attacks while maintaining excellent uniformity. For integers,
for small values, making integer-keyed dicts essentially free to hash.
Python randomizes hash seeds at interpreter startup (PYTHONHASHSEED) so hash values are not stable across processes. Never serialize a Python hash value and expect it to match in another run.

Think of a hash function as a library's cataloging system: given a book title, it calculates a shelf number in one step. As long as the formula is consistent and spreads books evenly, you find any book in constant time — no browsing required.

cards.title: Hash Table Basics
cards.teaser: An array plus a hash function equals O(1) lookup. Here's why that combination works.

runs.text: is a data structure that pairs an underlying array with a hash function. To store a key-value pair, the table hashes the key to find an index, then writes the value into that array slot. To retrieve a value, it hashes the key again and reads from the same index — one computation, one array access.

The array provides O(1) random access by index. The hash function provides the mapping from arbitrary key space to array indices. Together they give you a data structure that behaves like a searchable array where the index is a meaningful key.

items.text: On lookup, repeat steps 1–2 and read slot 7 — always slot 7.

runs.text: The array must be larger than the number of entries stored. A full array means every slot has a key, collisions become unavoidable, and performance degrades from O(1) toward O(n). The ratio of entries to capacity is the load factor — covered in card 4.

Imagine a coat check where the attendant computes your coat's slot number from your ticket — always the same slot, computed instantly. Checking in and checking out are both one step. The magic isn't the storage; it's having a formula that maps your ticket to a slot without searching.

cards.title: Collision Resolution
cards.teaser: Two keys, same slot. Chaining and open addressing are the two ways the world handles this.

runs.text: occurs when two different keys hash to the same array index. With a finite array and an infinite key space, collisions are mathematically inevitable. The strategy for handling them determines the practical performance of the hash table.

each array slot holds a linked list (or small dynamic array). All keys that hash to the same index are appended to that slot's list. Lookup requires scanning the chain. Chains can grow arbitrarily, so worst case is O(n), but average case with a good hash function and moderate load is O(1).
all entries live directly in the array — no linked lists. On collision, the table probes for the next available slot using a deterministic probe sequence. Common strategies:
(probe step is a second hash function of the key).

items.text: Chaining is simpler to implement and handles high load gracefully, but wastes memory on pointer overhead and breaks CPU cache locality.
Open addressing has excellent cache locality (all data in one contiguous array) but degrades sharply above ~70% load because probing chains grow long.

runs.text: Python's dict uses open addressing with a pseudo-random probe sequence — not linear probing — which avoids the primary clustering problem that makes linear probing slow at high load.

Chaining is like a parking lot where each space has a stack of cars — you get to your space instantly but then have to dig through the stack. Open addressing is like a parking lot where you keep trying adjacent spaces until you find one free — faster when it's empty, frustrating when it's full.

cards.title: Load Factor and Rehashing
cards.teaser: The ratio that predicts when your hash table turns from fast to slow — and what happens when it does.

runs.text: (λ) of a hash table is defined as:
λ = number of stored entries / array capacity

As λ increases, the probability of collision rises and performance degrades. For chaining, performance stays acceptable well above λ = 1 (more entries than slots). For open addressing, performance degrades sharply above λ ≈ 0.7 — above that threshold, probing sequences become long and cache misses multiply.

is the process of growing the array to bring the load factor back down. The table allocates a new, larger array (typically 2× the old capacity), then re-inserts every existing entry into the new array using the new modulus. Rehashing costs O(n) but happens infrequently enough that insertion is O(1) amortized — the same argument as dynamic array growth.

items.text: CPython's dict triggers rehashing when the table exceeds 2/3 full (λ > 0.67).
Java's HashMap defaults to a load factor of 0.75.
New capacity is typically chosen to be prime (in chaining-based designs) or a power of two (in open-addressing designs using bitwise masking instead of modulo).

runs.text: Pre-sizing a dict in Python with dict.fromkeys() or passing an initial size hint avoids mid-insertion rehashing. For a dict you know will hold 1 million entries, the first rehash will copy all previous entries — multiple times if you start small.

A hash table is like a restaurant. When it's 10% full, you're seated immediately. When it's 95% full, the host has to search for an available table — and the search takes longer the fuller it gets. Rehashing is like moving to a bigger building before things get too crowded, accepting the one-time moving cost for a long run of fast seating.

cards.title: Python dict Internals
cards.teaser: CPython's dict is not a textbook hash table — compact layout, insertion-order guarantees, and SIMD probing are what make it production-grade.

runs.text: : the next probe index is computed as
is derived from the high bits of the hash. This ensures full coverage of the array without the clustering problems of linear probing.

: a small sparse array of indices pointing into a dense array of (hash, key, value) entries. This eliminated the memory wasted by sparse arrays of full entries and, as a side effect, produced insertion-order iteration — formalized as a language guarantee in Python 3.7.

items.text: sparse, holds 1–8 byte integers pointing into the entries array. Size grows in powers of two.
dense, holds (cached_hash, key, value) triples in insertion order.
CPython 3.11+ uses SIMD vectorized comparison for the probe loop on supported hardware, further accelerating lookups.

runs.text: dict caches the hash of each key at insertion time. On lookup, it first compares cached hashes (a cheap integer compare) before calling __eq__. This means key equality is only tested when hashes collide — keeping the common case fast.

Old dict: a sparse spreadsheet where most cells are empty and each cell holds the full (key, value) record. New compact dict: a directory (sparse, small) pointing into a packed ledger (dense, ordered). The directory stays small and cache-friendly; the ledger preserves insertion order naturally.

cards.title: __hash__ and __eq__ Contract
cards.teaser: Two methods, one unbreakable rule: objects that compare equal must hash equal.

runs.text: Python's hash table protocol requires every hashable object to implement two methods in a way that satisfies the

items.text: If a == b then hash(a) == hash(b).
This is mandatory. Violating it causes keys to become unfindable after insertion.
If hash(a) == hash(b) it does NOT follow that a == b.
Hash collisions are expected and handled by the collision resolution mechanism.

runs.text: CPython enforces one consequence automatically: if you define
, making instances unhashable. This prevents the silent correctness bug of inheriting a hash that is inconsistent with the new equality.

Hashing a tuple of the fields used in
is idiomatic and correct — Python's tuple hash combines component hashes in a way that avoids naive collisions like

Never mutate an object's hash-relevant fields while it is stored as a dict key or set member. The object will be stored at index hash(old_state) % cap but is now findable only via hash(new_state) % cap — a different slot. The entry effectively disappears.

The contract is a one-way promise: equal objects must share a postcode (hash), but sharing a postcode doesn't mean you're the same person (equality). The table uses the postcode to find the neighborhood, then checks identity door by door. Break the postcode rule and the mail never arrives.

cards.title: Hashable vs Unhashable Types
cards.teaser: Why you can use a string or tuple as a dict key but not a list — and how to work around it.

runs.text: method consistent with it. The requirement for stability means: the hash value must not change during the object's lifetime. Mutable objects whose value can change cannot safely promise stability — hence Python's design:

items.text: int, float, complex, str, bytes, bool, None, tuple (if all elements are hashable), frozenset, user-defined classes (by default, using id-based hash)
list, dict, set — all mutable containers

runs.text: User-defined class instances are hashable by default: hash() returns id(self) // 16, and equality is identity (is). This breaks down when you override __eq__ — Python automatically sets __hash__ = None to protect you.

A hashable object is like a person with a permanent Social Security number. An unhashable object is like a person who changes their name, address, and face daily — the filing system can't give you a stable slot for someone who won't stay the same.

cards.title: set and frozenset
cards.teaser: A hash table with no values — pure membership testing in O(1), and the immutable variant that can live inside another set.

runs.text: is a hash table where each slot stores only a key — no associated value. This gives O(1) average-case membership testing (
), O(1) add, and O(1) discard. The same collision-resolution and rehashing mechanisms as
Set operations map directly to efficient hash-table algorithms:
is an immutable, hashable variant of

. Because it cannot change after creation, it satisfies the hash contract and can be used as a dict key or as an element of another set. Use it to represent a fixed group of items that needs to be treated as an atomic, comparable unit.

The most common performance mistake: checking membership in a list with 'if x in my_list' is O(n). If you perform this check repeatedly, convert to a set once: seen = set(my_list). Now every lookup is O(1).

A set is a dict with the value column torn out. You're not storing what something is worth — just whether it exists. Membership questions (is this person on the guest list?) answer in one step regardless of list size. frozenset is the laminated, read-only version you can tape to the wall and reference from multiple places.

cards.title: O(1) Average vs O(n) Worst Case
cards.teaser: Hash tables are almost always fast — but adversarial keys can make them catastrophically slow.

runs.text: , assuming a good hash function and moderate load factor. The average-case analysis assumes keys hash uniformly across slots, so each slot holds O(1) entries.

The worst case is O(n): if every key hashes to the same slot, the hash table degenerates to a linked list (chaining) or a full linear scan (open addressing). For random data, the probability of this is astronomically small. For

an attacker who knows the hash function can craft a payload (e.g., an HTTP form with thousands of keys that all collide) to degrade a server's dict operations from O(1) to O(n²) for n keys — a denial-of-service with a small request.

items.text: Python's defense: hash randomization (PYTHONHASHSEED) since Python 3.3. The seed changes each interpreter startup, so an attacker cannot pre-compute colliding keys without knowing the seed.
Java's defense: switch to tree-structured buckets (red-black tree) when a bucket exceeds 8 entries (Java 8+), capping worst-case lookup at O(log n).

runs.text: For security-sensitive key hashing (e.g., building a hash table from user-supplied input in a long-running process), use hmac.new(secret, key).digest() rather than the built-in hash(), which — despite randomization — is not designed as a cryptographic function.

O(1) average is like a GPS-guided parking system that gets you to an open spot in one trip — almost always. O(n) worst case is what happens when a prankster spray-paints all the GPS signs to point to the same spot: suddenly everyone is circling the same row. Hash randomization is like changing the GPS codes every morning so the prankster can't plan ahead.

cards.title: Hash Table Use Cases
cards.teaser: Caching, deduplication, and counting — three patterns that appear in almost every non-trivial program.

runs.text: Hash tables are the most frequently reached-for data structure in everyday programming because they convert O(n) membership tests and O(n) duplicate checks into O(1) operations. Three patterns dominate:
store the result of expensive computations keyed by their inputs.
are dict-backed. HTTP caches, DNS caches, and database query caches are all hash tables at the data-structure level.
track which items have been seen.
seen = set(); [seen.add(x) or x for x in items if x not in seen]
preserves order while deduplicating in O(n) total. The naive list-based approach is O(n²).
all work. Powers word counts, event histograms, and group-by aggregations.

Two-sum and its variants (find two numbers that add to a target) are solved in O(n) with a dict: for each x, check if target - x is already in the dict, then add x. Recognizing 'check then store' as a hash table pattern is a core interview skill.

Every time you find yourself looping through a list to check whether something is already there, you're doing O(n) work that a set or dict could do in O(1). The hash table is not a special-purpose tool — it's the default answer for 'have I seen this before?' and 'how many times have I seen this?'

cards.title: Bloom Filter
cards.teaser: A hash table that trades perfect accuracy for radical memory efficiency — it never lies about absence, but sometimes lies about presence.

runs.text: is a probabilistic data structure for membership testing that uses a bit array of size
independent hash functions. To insert an element, hash it
bits to 1. To test membership, hash the element

items.text: if the filter says 'not present', the element is definitely absent.
if the filter says 'present', the element is probably present but might not be — bits set by other elements can coincidentally match.
Space: O(m) bits regardless of how many elements are inserted — often 8–10 bits per element for a 1% false positive rate.
No deletion (standard variant) — clearing a bit might unset it for another element that also set it.

runs.text: Real-world uses: Google Chrome's Safe Browsing (check URLs against a local bloom filter before querying the server), Cassandra and RocksDB (skip SSTables that definitely don't contain a key), CDN edge caches (avoid backend lookups for definitely-missing resources).

A Bloom filter for 1 million URLs with 1% false positive rate requires roughly 10 MB — compared to storing 1 million average-length URLs verbatim (hundreds of MB). The tradeoff is accepting rare false positives in exchange for this compression.

A Bloom filter is a bouncer who stamps a shared card rather than keeping a guest list. When you arrive, they check your stamp — if it's not there, you're definitely not on the list. If it is there, you're probably on the list, but someone else's stamp might have landed in the same spot. Occasionally an innocent person gets turned away; never a listed guest.

cards.title: Consistent Hashing
cards.teaser: The hash ring that lets distributed systems add or remove nodes without reshuffling everything.

runs.text: changes: adding or removing one server remaps nearly every key, invalidating caches and causing a thundering herd of re-fetches.

solves this by mapping both keys and servers onto a fixed-size ring (typically [0, 2³²) or [0, 2⁶⁴)). Each server occupies one or more points on the ring. A key is assigned to the first server encountered by walking clockwise from the key's hash position. When a server is added or removed, only the keys between the new/removed server and its predecessor are remapped — O(k/n) keys rather than O(k).

items.text: each physical server is placed at multiple points on the ring under different hash seeds. This smooths load distribution and reduces variance when nodes have heterogeneous capacity.
Used by: Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Redis Cluster, most CDN edge routing systems.

runs.text: The data structure backing the ring lookup is typically a
of server positions, with binary search to find the successor — O(log n) per key assignment, where n is the number of virtual nodes.

Consistent hashing is one of the few cases where hash tables alone are insufficient. The ring lookup requires ordered structure (binary search on sorted positions), making it a hybrid: hash function for key placement, sorted array or tree for server lookup.

Imagine a clock face where servers sit at specific hours and keys land on random minute marks. Each key belongs to the first server clockwise from it. Add a new server at 3:00 — only the keys between 2:00 (the previous server) and 3:00 move. Remove the 6:00 server — only its keys migrate to 7:00. Everything else is undisturbed. This is why distributed caches survive server churn without cascading misses.
